sections.title: Paris events
sections.content:
• Tonight and tomorrow: Sarah Kay at 38Riv. The singer closes a three-night residency with two sets tonight, 4 August, and tomorrow, 5 August, at 19:30 and 21:30. 38Riv Jazz Club, 38 rue de Rivoli, Paris 4e; €19–24 online / €22–27 at the door. The programme mixes standards and original material, so this is the most immediate option if you want a compact seated jazz set rather than a late jam. Event and booking

  • Jam Session Jazz with Ananda Brandão — Wednesday 5 August. 38Riv, 23:00–01:30; €6–9, reservation advised. A short opening set leads into an open session with piano, double bass and drums available. It is a cheaper, less curated alternative to the earlier Sarah Kay sets and should be better if you want to hear the local scene rather than one finished programme. Official listing

  • Elisa Lécuyer tells the story of Betty Carter — Saturday 8 August. 38Riv; 15:00 and 17:00; €14–17 online / €17–20 on site. The format sits between concert and lecture, using Carter’s unusually elastic timing, fragmented phrasing and improvisational independence as the centre of the programme rather than presenting a generic vocal-jazz tribute. Event and booking

  • Free ongoing exhibition: “Coney Island Queen.” Photographs by Ludivine Combe are installed on the Berges de Seine, Rampe Châtelet, through 30 August. The series uses expired film to document Coney Island’s beach, performers and visitors; it is an easy detour rather than a destination requiring a fixed time slot. Exhibition page

sections.title: CS and AI developments
sections.content:
Hallucination may appear as an attention head breaking its usual role

A new VLM preprint, Role-Break in Attention Heads, asks whether hallucination has a model-agnostic internal signature. Instead of pooling all attention activity together, the method preserves the identity of each head and measures how its use of visual, textual and generated context deviates from its normal behaviour on faithful outputs. The authors call these localized deviations role-breaks.

The useful result is not merely another hallucination score. Once head identity is retained, the signal is reportedly readable by a linear detector with fewer than 5,000 features and no VLM fine-tuning; across six VLMs and four benchmarks, the authors report 93.23 mean AUROC. A small intervention study also suggests the flagged tokens can be acted on rather than only diagnosed after generation. This is still a fresh preprint and benchmark transfer is not operational reliability, but the architecture is attractive: diagnose failure through a structured internal representation instead of adding a second large verifier. Paper

CorrelationFlow removes training from LiDAR scene-flow estimation

CorrelationFlow takes the opposite direction from the learned monoculture around LiDAR scene flow. It converts successive point clouds into bird’s-eye-view occupancy images, groups points with connected-component labelling, then estimates object motion by finding the displacement that maximizes correlation. A sparse version matches compact occupancy descriptors at boundary keypoints using only one pair of sweeps.

That formulation gives up learned semantics but avoids inheriting a training distribution’s sensor and motion assumptions. The authors report second place among unsupervised methods in the multi-domain Argoverse 2 2026 Scene Flow Challenge and comparatively graceful degradation at long range. The broader lesson is relevant beyond autonomous driving: when the output is constrained by geometry, a classical decomposition can be more robust and inspectable than scaling an end-to-end network around the wrong abstraction. Paper

sections.title: Technical idea: taking a distributed snapshot without stopping the system
sections.content:
Suppose several services are passing money, jobs or tokens while you try to record “the current global state.” Reading each service one after another can create an impossible picture: a transfer may already have left process A but not yet appear in process B, so the snapshot seems to have lost it. Pausing every process would solve the problem, but distributed systems often cannot tolerate a global stop or even agree on one simultaneous instant.

The Chandy–Lamport snapshot algorithm records a causally consistent cut while the computation continues:

  1. An initiating process records its local state, then sends a special marker on every outgoing FIFO channel before sending further application messages.
  2. When another process sees its first marker, it records its own state, treats that incoming channel as empty, and forwards markers on its outgoing channels.
  3. For each other incoming channel, it records all messages received after its own local snapshot but before that channel’s marker. Those messages are the channel’s in-flight state.

The result need not be a wall-clock instant that every machine literally occupied together. It is a meaningful reachable global state containing each process state plus the messages crossing the cut. That is enough for checkpointing and for detecting stable properties—conditions that, once true, remain true—such as completed computation, lost tokens or deadlock. The deeper idea is that a consistent observation boundary can be encoded through message ordering; synchronized clocks are not required. Original 1985 paper

sections.title: Non-CS science: a wound scaffold that cells mechanically unlock
sections.content:
A new biomaterials study replaces scheduled drug release with cell-triggered release. The scaffold carries DNA aptamers—short strands selected to bind particular proteins. These aptamers capture growth factors already present in an injury, blood product or surrounding cells and hold them in an inhibited state. When a cell adheres and pulls on the scaffold, its traction force changes the aptamer’s shape and releases the growth factor locally at the point of contact.

The attraction is dosage and logistics. Rather than flooding a wound with manufactured recombinant proteins, the material harvests the patient’s own signals and activates them only where cells exert force. The researchers report vascularization in rat femur models, reduced wound diameter in mouse skin, and ex-vivo tests in human skin, using growth-factor quantities orders of magnitude below current clinical standards. The unmodified DNA constructs also remained functional long enough in enzyme-rich wounds to produce an effect.

This remains preclinical: the human tissue was outside the body, not a patient trial, and scaffold stiffness, degradation, immune response and activation across different cell types still need optimization. If it translates, however, the practical gain could be substantial—room-temperature, mechanically activated dressings or implants that avoid recombinant-protein manufacturing, repeated dosing and some cold-chain requirements. Open-access study

sections.title: Geopolitics and political economy
sections.content:
• UN succession: the Security Council is targeting 21 August for a second straw poll to replace António Guterres. Rebeca Grynspan emerged as the narrow early leader, but the decisive stage comes later, when colour-coded ballots reveal whether a permanent member is casting a veto-like “discourage” vote. A candidate ultimately needs nine Council votes and no P5 veto, so early plurality support is much less important than being acceptable across rival blocs. Reuters

  • Brazil: the Workers’ Party confirmed Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s seventh presidential run ahead of the 4 October election. Lula is framing rare minerals, defence industry and electronic voting as sovereignty questions, while party officials warn about foreign-supported bot campaigns and political endorsements for Flávio Bolsonaro from abroad. The material contest is not only left versus right: it is also over whether tariffs, platform manipulation and external executive pressure can alter coalition-building inside Latin America’s largest economy. AP

  • Taiwan: Defence Minister Wellington Koo said exchanges with the U.S. Pacific Command are “far closer than many people imagine” and are being used to improve readiness for scenarios including blockade. The important signal is operational integration below the threshold of formal alliance: common planning and military exchange can deepen while Washington preserves diplomatic ambiguity and Beijing treats the same activity as foreign intervention. Reuters

  • Ukraine: former commander-in-chief and current ambassador to Britain Valery Zaluzhnyi said he sees no realistic prospect of Ukraine entering NATO and argued that its armed forces lack required capabilities such as missile defence and space systems. Because NATO and EU membership remain constitutional goals, this is more than technical criticism: a highly trusted former commander is publicly separating long-term Western alignment from near-term alliance membership, increasing pressure to define credible security guarantees outside accession. Reuters

sections.title: Marxist fragment
sections.content:
“supplying capital with weapons against the revolts of the working-class.”

— Karl Marx, Capital, Volume I, Chapter 15, “The Strife Between Workman and Machine,” Samuel Moore and Edward Aveling translation. Primary text

Marx is discussing inventions introduced after strikes, including machinery designed to reduce employers’ dependence on a particular group of skilled workers. His claim is narrower and stronger than “technology destroys jobs”: the direction and timing of technical change can be selected through class conflict. A machine’s physical productivity and its managerial function—disciplining labour, weakening bargaining power or reorganizing skill—are analytically distinct, even when embodied in the same device.

This also prevents a romantic reading of machinery itself as the enemy. Marx’s target is its capitalist employment: social knowledge is materialized in machinery, but ownership determines who commands that knowledge and who absorbs the transition cost. Contemporary automation debates often measure output and headcount while omitting this third variable—how a technical system redistributes control over the labour process.

sections.title: Two philosophy and political fragments
sections.content:
David Hume: rule ultimately depends on organized belief

“It is therefore, on opinion only that government is founded.”

— David Hume, “Of the First Principles of Government,” Essays, Moral and Political. Primary text

Hume begins from the numerical puzzle that the governed usually outnumber the governors. A ruler’s direct force reaches little beyond one body; armies, officials and taxpayers must continue acting as if authority is rightful, useful or at least generally obeyed. “Opinion” here is not soft public relations opposed to material power. It includes expectations about interest, legitimacy and what others will do, all of which can be reproduced by institutions and coercion. The useful implication is that state capacity is partly a coordination equilibrium: force works because organized groups expect other organized groups to comply.

Edmund Burke: systems that cannot reform cannot preserve themselves

“A state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation.”

— Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790). Text

Burke is often reduced to defence of inherited order, but this sentence states a cybernetic point: an institution that cannot adjust to altered conditions accumulates pressure until preservation becomes impossible. The conservative conclusion is controlled reform; a revolutionary can accept the diagnosis while rejecting the proposed pace. The sharper question is therefore not “change or stability,” but which institutions can absorb conflict through reform and which make rupture the only remaining adjustment mechanism.

sections.title: French usage: ça ne mange pas de pain
sections.content:
Ça ne mange pas de pain means that an action costs little, demands little effort or carries little risk—roughly “it can’t hurt” or “there’s no harm in trying.”

  • Envoie-lui un message, ça ne mange pas de pain.
    Send them a message; it can’t hurt.
  • J’ai pris une capture d’écran, ça mange pas de pain.
    I took a screenshot; no harm in that.

In ordinary speech, ne is commonly dropped. The expression does not necessarily mean literally free: it can refer to a cheap precaution or an easy extra step. It can also sound mildly dismissive, as though the proposal is worth doing mainly because it is harmless rather than because it is likely to work. Larousse, manger

sections.title: Music corner
sections.content: Three deliberately separated lanes: a Czech symphony, composed minimalist jazz and instrumental hip-hop.

items.label: Classical
items.piece: Zdeněk Fibich — Symphony No. 1 in F major, Op. 17
items.description: A full symphonic rotation after Gade’s chamber writing. Fibich sits near the Dvořák–Smetana corridor without sounding like a derivative nationalist postcard: the first movement begins with pastoral woodwind colour, then builds a broad, clearly returned thematic architecture; the alla romanza slow movement gives the melody more weight as it moves from winds into strings and brass. The likely fit is the same combination that worked in Novák—legible melody, orchestral warmth and structural payoff—while remaining more tightly symphonic and less suite-like.

items.label: Jazz
items.description: Piano, saxophone and drums organize the piece around a repeated figure that gradually gains rhythmic pressure and harmonic mass. It is closer to a composed arc than an open-ended solo vehicle: the repetition functions as propulsion rather than ambience, while the saxophone provides a clear foreground voice. This tests whether the pulse and coherence that worked in GoGo Penguin can land more strongly with a darker, more cumulative arrangement.

items.label: Other
items.description: Instrumental hip-hop built around a warm, cyclical sample, clipped drums and a compact melodic arc. The loop stays stable, but phrasing and texture keep it in the foreground rather than turning it into background ambience. It tests a beat-driven lane outside jazz-trio and electronic-process writing while retaining the melodic clarity and coherent shape that tend to work best.

sections.title: Unrelated fact: reindeer retune the mirror behind their retina every winter
sections.content:
Arctic reindeer have a reflective layer behind the retina called the tapetum lucidum, the same general structure that produces eyeshine in cats. In summer it appears gold or turquoise and reflects much of the incoming light back out along a relatively direct path. In winter it becomes deep blue, and less light escapes immediately from the eye.

Months of dilated pupils are thought to raise pressure inside the eye and compress collagen fibres in the tapetum, changing the spacing that determines which wavelengths it reflects. The winter configuration scatters light through the photoreceptors for longer, trading some sharpness for sensitivity during prolonged Arctic twilight. This is not an iris-colour change; the eye is seasonally reconfiguring an optical component behind the retina to match its environment. UCL overview · Royal Society research summary

sections.title: Puzzle: Penney’s non-transitive coin game
sections.content:
Alice chooses the three-flip pattern HHT. After seeing her choice, Bob chooses a different three-flip pattern. A fair coin is then tossed repeatedly until either selected pattern first appears as three consecutive results; that player wins.

Question: What pattern should Bob choose to maximize his chance of winning, and what is that probability?

The catch is that all eight length-three patterns have probability 1/8 on any fixed block of three tosses. The advantage comes from how occurrences can overlap across time, and from the fact that one player’s near-completion can create the other player’s full pattern first.

Hint: try choosing a pattern whose last two symbols are Alice’s first two symbols. Background and interactive explanation
